newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: U.N. official calls for Cambodian truth commission.
newsitem.headline: U.N. official calls for Cambodian truth commission.

text.p: U.N. human rights officials believe Cambodia should set up some form of truth commission to ensure that the lessons of its brutal recent past are not lost on future generations.

The United Nations' special representative on human rights for Cambodia, Thomas Hammarberg, said last year's amnesty of former top Khmer Rouge cadre Ieng Sary raised fears the horrors of the 1975-79 Khmer Rouge regime and those responsible would be forgotten.
Hammarberg, contacted in his Stockholm office late on Wednesday, said truth commissions in South Africa and Latin America had helped clarify the past and start a real healing process.

"My suggestion was that the Cambodian authorities would consider studying some examples in other countries to see how they have dealt with it. Chile and South Africa would be two cases of specific interest," he told Reuters.

"I don't want to recommend one specific model, but I do want to recommend that the issue is not just brushed under the carpet because it will come back and that would be a very bad message when it comes to human rights for future generations."
South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission was set up last year to probe human rights violations during 30 years of race conflict.
Hammarberg said something new and specific for Cambodia might have to be created, adding that any entity would have to be independent and might need the help of overseas advisors and lawyers.
Hammarberg is expected to present his recommendation formally in a report to the annual meeting of the U.N. Commission on Human Rights in Geneva next month.

"The partial amnesty granted in September 1996 through a royal decree should not exclude the possibility of establishing a truth commission to clarify facts and assign responsibility," said a draft of the report, seen by Reuters.
Co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen persuaded King Norodom Sihanouk to pardon Ieng Sary, who had stalled peace talks after splitting with Khmer Rouge hardliners in August.
Ieng Sary was pardoned from a 1979 death sentence handed down in absentia for his role in the deaths of more than one million people during the brutal regime of Pol Pot.
Thousands of guerrillas have since defected to the government, but he is the only top leader to do so. The government has said it would accept others but never Pol Pot, whose whereabouts are unknown.
The U.S.-funded Cambodia Genocide Programme said last month it had enough new evidence in the past two years to implicate clearly the Khmer Rouge leaders in crimes against humanity.
"I don't think there will ever be a trial of the Khmer Rouge leadership," said a U.N. human rights worker in Cambodia, but added: "If something is feasible, it is a truth commission."
Justice ministry officials could not be reached for comment.
Information Minister Ieng Mouly said on Thursday he supported a truth commission in principle but would still like to see top Khmer Rouge leaders brought to trial one day.
"I think any action, any decision to find the evidence of the genocide is welcome," said parliamentary human rights commission chief Kem Sokha, who also favoured a later trial.
